executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is the fragility of institutional authority — whether in technology, politics, or geopolitics — and the fierce competition to fill the vacuum left behind. Google's displacement of OpenAI as the leading consumer AI platform, covered in both The Economist and the New York Times, signals a power realignment at the heart of the technology industry, one with profound implications for how billions of people access information and how regulatory frameworks will need to adapt. On Capitol Hill, Republican infighting over Trump's budget package reveals that even a unified government struggles to exercise coherent institutional will, a theme that echoes directly into Foreign Affairs' examination of crumbling global peace pillars and whether Trump's foreign policy reflects strategy or improvisation. MIT Technology Review's report on researchers suing the Trump administration over online safety further underscores that the battle for institutional legitimacy is being fought simultaneously in courtrooms, congressional chambers, and corporate boardrooms. Taken together, today's content makes clear that the central story of this moment is not any single policy or product launch, but rather a systemic contest over who holds authority — and on what terms — across the most consequential domains of modern life.

newsletters.title: Tech researchers are suing the Trump administration over the future of online safety

items.headline: Tech researchers are suing the Trump administration over the future of online safety
items.blurb:
For months, the Trump administration has been going after researchers who study and try to counter hate speech, harassment, propaganda, and disinformation online. Now, some of those researchers are fighting back.

In a new lawsuit, they're seeking to strike down a visa restriction policy against "foreign officials and other persons" announced last year by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

They say the policy violates the speech and due process rights of foreign-born workers whose "work supports greater moderation of content on the [tech] platforms."

items.headline: Climate tech companies are pivoting to critical minerals
items.blurb:
We're over a year into the second Trump administration, and support for climate causes in the US is weak. But climate tech companies are finding ways to survive and even thrive in this new environment, including by looking beyond decarbonization.

One example is Boston Metal. The startup has raised a $75 million round to produce critical metals, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

The company is best known for its efforts to clean up steel production, an industry that's responsible for about 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the new focus and fresh funds could help it survive a period of waning support for industrial decarbonization.

items.headline: Can AI learn to understand the world?
items.blurb:
As the limits of LLMs become clearer, researchers are developing a new kind of AI designed to understand the physical environment: world models.

Recent developments from Google DeepMind, Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, and Yann LeCun's new startup have pushed these systems to the forefront of AI. At an exclusive virtual event today, MIT Technology Review will examine the progress—and what comes next.

items.headline: Brandon Dwyer quote on being a walk-on
items.blurb: "Being a walk-on taught me that true fulfillment comes from contributing to the team's success, even when personal rewards are limited."

items.headline: Ally Sentnor quote on grace and consistency
items.blurb: "I try to give myself grace and remember that not every day will feel like 100 percent. At the same time, I recognize that building a strong foundation and achieving lasting success requires consistency — even on the days when I'm not at my best. I remind myself that growth is still possible on hard days, even if they aren't my most productive."

items.headline: Rafael Nadal quote on enduring and accepting
items.blurb: "Enduring means accepting. Accepting things as they are and not as you would wish them to be, and then looking ahead, not behind."

items.headline: Rick Pitino quote on adversity
items.blurb: "You don't f---ing get down when things go wrong. You dig and get tougher. Your whole life is going to be f---ing adversity. Learn how to deal with it."

items.headline: Leonard Marshall quote on being a gamer
items.blurb: "What will you do when you're the tiredest? When your mind can't think or fathom? When you can't seem to muster enough energy to fight one more play? ... Who will you be in that moment? And if you're a gamer — if you're a guy who rises to the occasion, takes on the challenge and meets it head on — it won't even matter to you. It will just be a moment in time."

items.headline: The theory of trust
items.blurb: Michael Gervais, a sports psychologist who has worked with the Seattle Seahawks, explained the three key components of the theory of trust: Leaders are consistent and the same over a glass of wine as they are in tense, high-stakes environments. They demonstrate benevolence to the people they lead. The last piece is ability. Can they back up what they say with evidence of their success? Gervais argues that the best leaders in sports check all three of those boxes.

items.headline: Worst-case scenarios
items.blurb: Most of the time, athletes talk about positive visualization. So I was interested when Rory McIlroy talked about how thinking about worst-case scenarios actually helped him remain calm. He'd imagine hitting a drive into the trees in a big tournament and then visualize what he would actually do: You go up there, and you figure it out. You're skillful enough to hit a punch shot out of the trees ... and get it out of the trees ... and get it up to the green ... and get it up and down ... and make a par ... and move on.

items.headline: "Don't seek comfort"
items.blurb: Former Pittsburgh Steelers coach Mike Tomlin used to tell his players this after tough losses. Tomlin's point: Don't look for relief. Don't look for an easy way to make yourself feel better during a tough time. Instead, he demanded that players seek accountability and face their mistakes head-on in order to learn from them.

breaking_digest.narrative:
On Capitol Hill, Republicans hit turbulence on the budget front as House members balked at provisions in Trump's spending package, forcing a delay in scheduled votes [2]. Separately, a federal panel approved Trump's arch plans, marking a procedural step forward for that initiative [4], while Democrats released a post-mortem on their 2024 electoral losses, placing primary blame on President Biden and broader structural failures within the party [5]. The Supreme Court also issued a significant ruling, allowing American citizens to pursue lawsuits over assets seized by Cuba in 1960, opening a long-dormant legal avenue for claimants [6].

In other news, Tennessee called off a scheduled execution after prison staff were unable to locate a viable vein on the condemned prisoner, halting the lethal injection process before it began [3]. Eli Lilly reported striking results from trials of an experimental weight-loss drug, with the company citing dramatic reductions in body weight among participants [7]. The day ended on a somber note with the death of NASCAR star Kyle Busch at age 41 [1].
